1:
They agree the city was doubly closed and disagree about why. Gill reports the Targum's iron doors and bars of brass and distinguishes the shutting within from the blocking without by Israel. Keil holds that the participles express the permanence of the situation and that the emphatic Hebrew form, combining active and passive, strengthens the idea, reinforced by the clause that no one was going out or in; the Greek and Latin versions keep the doubling. Calvin takes the sealing as ordinary wartime vigilance, the inhabitants watching so as not to be surprised, so that stratagem was excluded and open force the only hope. Henry makes the cause moral: it shut up itself, fortified by art and nature and by the obstinacy of inhabitants who agreed never to surrender nor sound a parley, thus hardened to their own destruction, the character he assigns to all who strengthen themselves against the Almighty. Clarke makes it a precaution: the king, finding the spies had escaped, kept the city shut by day as well as night, having provisions to stand a siege.

On where the chapter division falls there is a majority. Ellicott reads the first verse parenthetically and the four following as the orders given Joshua by the captain of the Lord's host. Keil says the same, and identifies the speaker as the prince of the army, the angel of Jehovah, frequently identified with Jehovah himself. Clarke agrees on the speaker and complains that the discourse begun at the end of the preceding chapter is here unnaturally divided; Gill calls him the same divine Person, the Captain of the Lord's host.

Henry and Keil weigh the tense of the promise. Keil notes that the giving refers to a purpose of God already resolved on though not yet fulfilled, and that the mighty men of valour stand in apposition to the city and its king. Henry presses it harder: not I will do it, but I have done it, all thy own as sure as if already in thy possession. He meets the difficulty that the city was devoted, so that neither Joshua nor Israel should be one mite the richer for it, and yet it is said to be given into their hand; we must reckon that most our own which we have an opportunity of honouring God with. Clarke adds from a later chapter that people of all seven Canaanitish nations may have been gathered in the city.

The manner of the siege occupies most of them. Henry observes that no trenches were opened, no batteries erected, no rams drawn up nor any military preparations made, and finds two reasons, to magnify God's power so that he might be exalted in his own strength and not that of instruments, and to put honour on the ark. Gill notes it was a procession, not the form of a siege, all the men of war meaning all above twenty. Wesley sets the circuit out of the reach of their arrows, and holds the course prescribed so they might learn to take new measures of things and not judge God's institutions by carnal reason. Calvin says the thing looked like nothing but child's play, yet was no improper test of faith, since God often conceals his might under weakness, and they gained more by trifling than by the most powerful engines; they had only to play the fool a short time, not inquire too subtly about the event, and cast on providence the danger that the city might sally out against their straggling lines. He adds that the instruments were not the silver trumpets of the sanctuary but merely rams' horns, contentment with which was the better proof of obedience. Clarke alone admits the text does not settle the order of march, some thinking they kept the order of the desert, others that soldiers went first, then priests, ark and people.
4:
What the seven trumpets were is contested. Gill notes the original word is jubilee rather than rams' horns, that some hold it means only the trumpets used in the jubilee year, and derives the name from the first inventor of musical instruments; rams' horns being objected to as solid and not hollow, as if they could not be bored. Clarke denies the sense outright: the Hebrew does not signify rams' horns, no ancient version but the Chaldee gives it that meaning, the instruments were evidently those used at the jubilee, probably of horn or silver, and he would render it the seven jubilee trumpets. Ellicott glosses them as trumpets of jubilee, of loud or joyful sound; Wesley the reverse. They were of the basest matter and the dullest sound, that the excellency of the power might be of God.

On the ark at the centre, Gill reports the opinion that it was carried to direct Israel to keep the law it contained, but prefers his own, that the design was to show the taking of the city owed all to God's power and presence. Ellicott reads the scene as a legal execution: the ark holds the written law, the armed men before it are its executioners, the priests who blow its heralds. Keil notes that the priests passed on before Jehovah rather than before the ark, whose significance derived entirely from its being the medium of his presence. The seven days are explained twice. Clarke says the time was lengthened so that besiegers and besieged might be more deeply impressed with the supernatural power; Ellicott makes the silence a lesson in the forbearance of God, who had waited generations while the iniquity of the land was not yet full, so that the shout was his signal that he would wait no longer, and no inapt figure of the shout at the Lord's second coming.

How the wall fell divides Clarke and Wesley. Clarke reports that several commentators, Jews and Christians, supposed the ground opened and the wall sank into the chasm, and answers that the text says nothing of it; the Hebrew, literally that the wall shall fall down under itself, means only that it fell from its very foundations, large breaches amply sufficing to admit the armed men and then the host. Wesley denies that all of it fell, which was unnecessary and might have given the people better opportunity of escaping; a considerable part fell where Israel might fitly enter, Rahab's house standing. He reads under it to mean it was not battered down with engines, which would have made part fall out of its place, but fell of its own accord where it had stood. God chose this way to try whether they would observe a precept that to human policy seemed foolish and believe a promise that seemed impossible: by faith, not by force, the walls fell down.

Keil settles the order of march. He explains the plural they said by Joshua proclaiming through the officers who issued his commands, and finds here the detail omitted earlier, the equipped man marching in front of the ark; against a modern he denies this means all the fighting men, since the men of war divide into the armed and the rearward, so the equipped is only one division. Gill takes the people addressed for women, children and men under twenty, the unarmed part. Wesley says the armed went to defend themselves and the ark should the enemy sally, and to execute the Lord's vengeance. Henry adds that they thought it no disparagement, though men of war, to be pioneers to the ark, and that the rearward was either a second armed body, the squadron that marched last in the wilderness, or the unarmed multitude following to grace the solemnity. Gill adds that the seventh day's protracted blast, unlike the short blasts before, was itself the people's token.
8:
Who marched at front and back is unsettled. Gill reports three Jewish commentators taking the armed men for the two and a half tribes Joshua brought over the river, but prefers all the armed men in the camp, with the standards of Judah and Ephraim. On the rearward Clarke offers four senses of the word: the rearward as the English has it; the baggage-carriers, needed on the seventh day when fighting was expected; those who carried the sacred articles belonging to the ark; or people merely following without observing any particular order. The Jews, he adds, think the division that always brought up the rear is meant. Wesley, setting the word against the armed men, makes it the unarmed people, desirous to be spectators.

The silence and the repetition are read as discipline. Wesley says shouting before the appointed time would have been ineffectual, discouraging the people and giving their enemies matter of insulting. Calvin presses harder: God seemed, by leading them so often round, not only to keep the matter in suspense but purposely to sport with their miseries, since they fatigued themselves to no purpose. Why not order a sudden attack, and why keep them silent to weariness? The happy fruit of the endurance teaches that there is nothing better than to leave the decisive moments at his disposal and not by our haste anticipate his providence, which, if we acquiesce not, we obstruct. God matched the shout to the priests' sounding, to prove that he is not pleased with impetuosity men manifest at their own hands but requires a regulated zeal, whose only rule is not to move tongue or feet or hands till he order; and the horns, Calvin adds, represented his authority. Gill takes Joshua's rising early on the second morning for the same diligence.

Two points of grammar cut opposite ways. Keil insists the text says the ark compassed the city, not that Joshua caused it to compass, the Hiphil being here active and not causative; Gill allows Kimchi's rendering, that Joshua caused the ark to compass it. Keil also defends the received verb form against an unnecessary emendation, and notes that the seventh day began at the dawning because seven circuits were to be made, in the manner prescribed before, which had become a right through precept and practice. Ellicott renders the participle literally, with a going and a blowing with the trumpets, and observes that the word priests is a Targum insertion.

The seventh day raises the sabbath. Gill reports that one Jewish authority makes it the sabbath, a common notion among them, adds that one of the seven days must have been, and quotes as remarkable the rabbinic saying that though they slew and burnt on the sabbath, he who commanded the sabbath commanded it profaned in the subduing of the city. Clarke grants that a sabbath fell within the week and that the host encompassed the city on it, and quotes the same saying, but denies any breach: they simply went round with the ark and the sounding priests, a religious procession at God's command in which no servile work was done. On that ground he answers the old objection that the God of the Hebrews showed a changeableness of disposition in commanding the sabbath kept sacred at one time and broken at another, and holds that no breach took place unless the day the city fell was itself the sabbath, which none can prove. He argues besides from the seven circuits that the city was small, the fighting men alone being near six hundred thousand and the people some millions, so that only a select number marched, a hundredth part of the force sufficing to reduce it.
16:
Wesley gives the shout four purposes: to testify faith in God's promise and thankfulness, to encourage themselves and their brethren, and to strike terror into their enemies. He and Henry agree that the city was given to be devoted to God, the first and perhaps the worst of all the cities of Canaan. Henry draws the inference: God gives it, and may direct it to what uses and clog it with what provisos he thinks fit. The city must be burnt and the lives in it sacrificed to the justice of God, no life ransomed on any terms; he appoints from whom as creatures they had received their lives and to whom as sinners they had forfeited them, and who may dispute his sentence? More of God was seen in the taking of this city than of any other, and therefore it must be more devoted to him; the severity would strike terror on the rest. Rahab alone is excepted, having distinguished herself by the kindness she showed and so distinguished by the speedy return of it.

On why the ban fell here they differ in emphasis. Calvin finds a peculiarity in the first city: God meant to enrich his people with spoil and settle them in cities they had not built, but this one was to be consecrated as a kind of first fruits, so he claims the buildings and moveable property as his own. It may have been irksome to pull down houses they might have dwelt in and destroy useful articles, but as they had not been required to fight they should yield the rewards of victory to him without grudging, since by his nod alone the walls fell and the courage of the citizens with them; and with equal right all the other cities might have been doomed, had he not granted them for habitations. Wesley adds two practical reasons beside the appropriation of firstfruits: lest soldiers glutted with the spoil of a rich city grow sluggish, and to strike the greater terror into the rest. Clarke alone supposes peace was offered the city first, the extermination following the rejection of that offer.

What the word means is worked out by Ellicott and Calvin. Ellicott renders it a devoted or accursed thing and shows both ideas combined in the sin offering, which is called most holy and yet, when offered for the priest or congregation, must be utterly consumed. Calvin distinguishes two senses in successive verses: of sacred oblations, that the thing devoted is renounced as completely as if annihilated, the Greek equivalent being anathema; in the caution about the camp, simply excision, perdition or death. He notes that God destined the metal vessels for the sanctuary and ordered all else consumed by fire. Clarke allows a milder sense elsewhere but total destruction here; Gill renders it simply devoted.

The treasure is treated last. Henry reports the Jewish reason for its consecration, that the city was taken on the sabbath, and offers his own: God would be honoured by the enriching of his tabernacle, provision made for the extraordinary expenses of his service, and Israel was taught not to set their hearts on worldly wealth, since God had promised a land flowing with milk and honey and not one abounding with silver and gold, that they might live comfortably and serve cheerfully without hoarding; they were to reckon what lay in God's house as truly their wealth as if it lay in their own. Calvin makes the same demand a pledge of gratitude, God content with it provided the people learned that all they called their own was the gift of his free liberality. On the forbidden spoil Henry has Joshua tell them they will be inclined to reach towards it and must check themselves from touching it, and remarks that he speaks as if he foresaw the sin recorded in the next chapter.
18:
Gill defines the offence as laying hold on, secreting and enjoying as one's own what was devoted to another use; Wesley explains how the whole camp could be involved, either by God punishing them for a sin they share, or, the camp having sins of its own, by his taking what occasion he sees fit. Wesley is exactest on the metals: images were excepted and utterly destroyed, the rest passed first through the fire, and it went wholly to the tabernacle, not to any private person or priest. Ellicott points to the parallel Midianite spoil; Clarke supplies a traveller's note that the Brahmins will receive gold and silver from any caste however degraded, but not food or garments.

Clarke reports that much learned labour has been spent proving the shouting the natural cause of the wall's falling, declines to refute it as lost time, and holds the relation supposes a supernatural interference, the trumpets and shouting being too contemptible to serve even as instruments in a natural account. Calvin praises the people twice over. They testified their fidelity by shouting, persuaded that what God commanded would not be in vain, and he, not letting them lose their labour, vindicated his word. The second virtue he rates no lower: they despised unlawful gain and cheerfully suffered the loss of all the plunder, though many minds must have asked why God destroyed all the wealth, why he envied them what he had given into their hand, and why he did not gladden them with the materials of thanksgiving.

The slaughter is defended by four and explained otherwise by a fifth. Calvin grants that killing without distinction of age or sex might seem an inhuman massacre had it not been executed by God's command, but holds that his just dooming of those nations ends all discussion, the more so since they had been borne with four hundred years till their iniquity was complete. Clarke argues the same in a line, that the Judge of all the earth cannot do wrong, and notes that nothing which breathed was spared, oxen, sheep and asses alike. Gill grounds it on capital crimes deserving death. Wesley pleads that the infants were guilty of original sin and otherwise at their creator's disposal, and that even had they been innocent it was a favour to take them early rather than leave them to the calamities their survivors faced. Ellicott gives a different reason for the animals: they died so Israel might not seem to slaughter for plunder, all ordered to mark the vengeance of God. Keil observes that at the other towns only the inhabitants were put to death, the cattle and booty falling to the conquerors.

Rahab's exemption raises two difficulties. Calvin asks how one family could be excepted when no mortal might change God's decision, answers that she bargained for impunity only by the Spirit's suggestion, the messengers being under no contrary obligation before the ban was declared, then offers a far easier solution: Israel exhorted all whom they attacked to surrender, holding out pardon, and the blinded nations obstinately refused, so Rahab alone was exempted. Gill raises the other, how the spies entered a house built on a wall fallen flat, reporting two answers: they had marked the place by the scarlet thread while circling, though then they did not properly go in, or only the wall facing the camp fell; Wesley says her house and its wall were left standing by special favour. On the family kept outside, Clarke and Wesley take them for unclean till they had abjured heathenism, been purified and circumcised; Calvin denies it was for safety, since they would have been received with the greatest favour and in a solitary place attacked more easily, and makes it a discipline of shame, lest by immediate mixing the thought of their impurity never occur. Ellicott renders the phrase literally, caused them to rest.
24:
Clarke turns the spoils into an argument: the people had no share, having had no hand in the conquest, God alone overthrew the city, and the spoils went only into his treasury, one proof, he says, that the people's voice did not bring the walls down. He notes that the Alexandrian Greek reads all the brass and iron for vessels, a reading in none of the collated manuscripts. Gill looks past the burning to the great city it was an emblem of, to be burnt with fire likewise.

What saving Rahab alive means is disputed. Gill reports that some read it of food and an inheritance, that Josephus says Joshua gave her fields and held her in honour, and that some make it his taking her to wife, rejected by one Jewish writer as foreign and by Gill because it was a prince of Israel, not Joshua, who married her. Keil identifies her with the woman of Christ's genealogy, traces the doubts to the same scruple over her calling that led the Chaldee translator to make her an innkeeper, prefers Jerome's answer, and takes the note that she dwelt in Israel unto this day for evidence of an early date, as Clarke does for the book. Ellicott gathers the New Testament witnesses to her faith and works, and observes that the Greek form of her name there is not the usual one, a difference in the original and not in the spelling. Wesley finds in her an exception to the command of rooting out the Canaanites, for any who had sincerely and seasonably cast off their wickedness.

The curse is read as memorial, prediction and imprecation. Calvin says the adjuration was to warn posterity that the city had been taken only by divine power; the ruins were to stand as a trophy, rebuilding being an erasure that would efface the miracle, the natural torpidity of men requiring such stimulants against burying divine favours in oblivion, the spectacle being an indirect censure of their ingratitude. He renders it as a picture: to lay the foundation in the firstborn is to cast forth a son to perish beneath the stones, to set the gates in the younger a building not to be raised without a son's death. Keil makes it the ban completed by oath, a memorial of God's justice sanctifying itself on the ungodly, and notes its rhythmical parallelism and the preposition of price. Wesley says Joshua made the people, or some in the name of all, swear for themselves and their successors, not from dislike of the place but by divine inspiration, and restricts the curse to the builder alone. Gill notes the adjuration was general; Clarke calls it a strange execration better considered as a prediction.

On the fulfilment they divide. Clarke offers two accounts, that the builder's children died one by one during the work, or that the history relates merely to its slow progress between the eldest son's birth and the youngest's, and prefers the first; he reckons the interval at five hundred and fifty years, Calvin at five hundred and twenty. Whether the site lay empty is disputed: Clarke identifies the city of palm trees with Jericho and infers from later notices that it was inhabited long before, Ellicott makes that identification only doubtfully, and Calvin supposes a second city built near but not on the former site, avoided while the memory of the curse remained. Ellicott adds that it appears to have been finally removed by a later prophet's intercession. Clarke closes with classical parallels for cursing rebuilders, and rests the miracle on the apostolic word that by faith the walls fell. Gill and Wesley end where the chapter does, with the Targum's reading that the Word of the Lord was Joshua's help, which both take for Christ; Wesley adds that nothing makes a man appear more truly great than the evidences of God's presence.
